docs.title: The Lockfile
docs.text:
The uv.lock file is a TOML file generated by uv next to pyproject.toml. It records exact dependency versions, their relationships, package sources, and download hashes across the project's supported operating systems and Python versions. It is kept under version control and updated and reviewed alongside pyproject.toml so development, CI, and production can reuse the same reviewed versions.

The uv lock command resolves the requirements declared in pyproject.toml and creates or updates the lockfile without creating a project virtual environment or installing packages. It may download package metadata, wheels, or source archives during resolution. It preserves existing locked versions where possible and leaves an up-to-date lockfile unchanged, even when newer versions are available.

uv lock

The following code block is an excerpt of uv.lock, with download entries and other packages omitted for readability. Each [[package]] entry describes a resolved package: FastAPI is locked to 0.115.14, which satisfies the declared range, and Starlette is one of its transitive dependencies. A package's dependencies list identifies the packages it requires, whose resolved versions are recorded in their own [[package]] entries. Here, FastAPI requires Starlette, which in turn requires AnyIO. The top-level version and revision describe the lockfile format, not the project's version.

version = 1
revision = 3
requires-python = ">=3.11"

[[package]]
name = "fastapi"
version = "0.115.14"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "pydantic" },
    { name = "starlette" },
    { name = "typing-extensions" },
]

[[package]]
name = "starlette"
version = "0.46.2"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "anyio" },
]

Commands that update the lockfile

uv lock, uv add, uv remove, uv sync, uv run, uv tree, and uv export create or update uv.lock as needed.

docs.title: Upgrade the Lockfile
docs.text:
The uv lock --upgrade command resolves all dependencies to the latest versions allowed by the constraints in pyproject.toml. Use --upgrade-package instead to upgrade a specific dependency while retaining other locked versions where possible.

Single DependencyAll Dependencies

Upgrade a single dependency to the latest version its constraint allows, retaining other locked versions where possible.

uv lock --upgrade-package fastapi

Upgrade all dependencies to the latest versions allowed by their declared ranges.

uv lock --upgrade

Install the updated versions into the project's virtual environment:

uv sync

docs.title: Validate the Lockfile
docs.text:
The uv lock --check command validates that the lockfile is in sync with pyproject.toml without modifying it. Use it in CI or before committing to catch outdated lockfiles:

uv lock --check

docs.title: Default Synchronization
docs.text:
Local Development

Use the default sync for day-to-day development. It keeps the virtual environment aligned with the project metadata and, by default, installs the project in editable mode with the configured default dependency groups.

The uv sync command prepares a project's Python environment by installing the dependency versions recorded in uv.lock. It creates an in-project virtual environment (.venv) if needed and installs, upgrades, downgrades, or removes packages to match the selected dependencies and dependency groups. If the lockfile is outdated relative to pyproject.toml, it re-locks automatically before installing.

DefaultDependency GroupAll Groups

Install dependencies from project.dependencies in pyproject.toml and the default dependency groups, including their transitive dependencies (packages those dependencies require). The dev group is included by default unless tool.uv.default-groups changes that selection.

uv sync

Include a dependency group alongside project.dependencies and the default groups. This example explicitly selects dev, which is normally already included by default.

uv sync --group dev

Install project.dependencies and all dependency groups, but not optional extras unless explicitly requested.

uv sync --all-groups

docs.title: Frozen Installs
docs.text:
Intermediate Docker Layers

Use frozen syncs in intermediate Docker layers or workspace builds when dependencies need to be installed before all project source files are available. Because --frozen skips lockfile freshness checks, validate the lockfile separately and run a final --locked sync once all project files are present. See uv's intermediate-layer guidance.

The uv sync --frozen command performs frozen installs that use the dependency versions recorded in an existing lockfile without checking whether it matches the declarations in pyproject.toml or updating it. Any dependency change in pyproject.toml is therefore not resolved into a new lockfile during the sync.

uv sync --frozen [--no-install-project] [--no-install-workspace]
  • --no-install-project: Skips installing the project itself while still installing its dependencies.
  • --no-install-workspace: Installs only dependencies, not workspace projects.

docs.title: Locked Installs
docs.text:
CI/CD and Production Builds

Locked, non-editable installs suit production targets and CI/CD steps that prepare deployment artifacts. Typical locations are GitHub Actions workflow files and Dockerfile build steps. Kubernetes Manifests can also run the command through container command and args fields, though installing dependencies during the image build avoids startup-time downloads.

The uv sync --locked command performs locked installs that prepare the project environment using the dependency versions recorded in uv.lock, while checking that the lockfile matches the declarations in pyproject.toml. If the lockfile is missing or stale, the command fails rather than changing it automatically, requiring it to be created or updated and reviewed before the build proceeds. The pyproject.toml must define a [build-system] for uv sync to install the project itself. See uv's editable installation guidance.

EditableNon-Editable

By default, uv sync installs the project and workspace members in editable mode, so imports use their source checkout and reflect source edits without reinstalling.

uv sync --locked

With --no-editable, the project is installed into the virtual environment as a regular Python package, so Python imports the installed files rather than your source files directly. The installed package can still be imported if you move or remove the source folder, however, editing source files does not change the installed version.

For example, a package named sync_demo on Python 3.12 is installed under .venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sync_demo/, alongside sync_demo-0.1.0.dist-info/, which stores its name, version, and other package information. A regular sync may reuse that installation. To apply your edits, use the optional --reinstall-package sync-demo flag to force rebuilding and reinstalling. Running a source file directly still executes your edited code.

uv sync --locked --no-editable [--reinstall-package sync-demo]

docs.title: Test Compatibility Ranges
docs.text:
Before writing a lockfile, uv resolves direct and transitive dependencies to find versions that satisfy all declared constraints. It does this automatically when dependencies are added, updated, or synchronized and, by default, selects the latest compatible version of each dependency.

For libraries, testing only against the latest versions is insufficient: a declaration such as fastapi>=0.100.0 claims compatibility with every version from 0.100.0 upward, not just the newest release.

All DependenciesDirect Dependencies

Install the lowest compatible versions for all direct and transitive dependencies:

uv sync --resolution lowest

Install the lowest compatible versions for direct dependencies only, keeping transitive dependencies at their latest:

uv sync --resolution lowest-direct

docs.title: Conflicting Extras
docs.text:
uv normally resolves extras together. When two features deliberately need incompatible versions, declare the conflict so they can be resolved separately. This example uses two mutually exclusive idna versions to make the behavior visible:

[project.optional-dependencies]
legacy = ["idna==3.9"]
modern = ["idna==3.10"]

[tool.uv]
conflicts = [[{ extra = "legacy" }, { extra = "modern" }]]

Synchronize one extra at a time; requesting both produces an error:

uv sync --extra legacy

docs.title: Inspect the Graph
docs.text:
Display the resolved dependency tree, showing which package pulled in which transitive dependency:

uv tree

docs.title: Export Dependencies
docs.text:
When another tool expects a requirements.txt, export one from the project's lockfile:

uv export --format requirements.txt -o requirements.txt

Keep pyproject.toml and uv.lock as the project's source of truth; regenerate the export after changing dependencies. For working directly with an existing requirements.txt, see Standalone Environments and Tools.

docs.title: Dependency Caching with uv
docs.text: uv caches package metadata, downloaded wheels, and wheels built from source. A project environment (.venv) is normally beside pyproject.toml; it is not the package cache. The Bob Follows the Cache notebook runs the same experiments as this section. Run the commands below from /workspace in the lab's Dev Container, in order. A first run needs network access.

docs.title: Applied Lab
docs.text: The lab locks NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib and builds a local uv-cache-demo wheel containing a generated 16 MiB synthetic matrix. Its fixture is deterministic and not a trained model. Downloaded numerical-library wheels make cache growth visible; the locally built wheel makes CI pruning visible. The container supplies uv 0.13.3 (for the centralized-environment preview), Python 3.12, and Jupyter, but does not install the project or populate its uv cache at startup. The separate CI workflow pins uv 0.11.1. The lab's UV_LINK_MODE=copy keeps installed files independent of the cache. The container's cache is separate from your host's.

docs.title: Environment Variables That Influence Cache Behavior
docs.text:
These variables configure where uv caches data, whether it can reuse it, and how it installs files from the cache. See the uv environment variable reference for the complete list.

Variable Cache behavior UV_CACHE_DIR Selects the shared cache directory instead of the system default; equivalent to --cache-dir. UV_NO_CACHE Uses a temporary cache for that invocation rather than the persistent cache; equivalent to --no-cache. UV_OFFLINE Disables network access, requiring cached or local packages; equivalent to --offline. UV_LINK_MODE Chooses clone (copy-on-write when supported), hardlink (shared files on one filesystem), copy (independent files), or symlink (depends on the cache). Defaults to clone on Linux/macOS and hardlink on Windows. UV_LOCK_TIMEOUT Sets how long uv waits for a cache lock, including when other uv processes are using the cache. UV_CONCURRENT_CACHE_READS Controls threads reading cached HTTP responses; defaults to 4.

docs.title: Commands That Populate the Cache
docs.text:
Package operations populate or reuse cache entries; cleanup commands remove them. For project locking and syncing, see Dependency Management with uv.

Command Effect on the cache uv pip install {pkg} Reuses or adds package metadata and wheels. --refresh revalidates cached data; --refresh-package {pkg} limits that to one package. uv add {pkg} Adds a dependency, resolves and synchronizes the project, and reuses or adds cached packages. uv sync Synchronizes a project from its lockfile, using or adding cached packages. uv tool install {tool} Installs a tool in its own environment while sharing uv's package cache. uv cache prune Removes unused entries and centralized project environments. With --ci, also removes prebuilt wheels and unzipped source distributions while retaining source-built wheels. uv cache clean [package] Removes all cache entries, or entries for only the named package.

docs.title: Build Configuration and Wheel Reuse
docs.text:
For a local package, tool.uv.cache-keys in pyproject.toml defines which build inputs invalidate a cached wheel. Keys replace uv's default checks: include every input that affects the build. A key containing only pyproject.toml, for example, may miss source-only changes. These configurations illustrate three ways to track inputs:

FilesGit CommitEnvironment Variable

Track the manifest and an additional dependency file used by the build.

[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { file = "requirements.txt" }]

Track the manifest and Git commit when the build depends on version control; add tags = true if tags affect it too. A commit key alone will not detect uncommitted source edits.

[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { git = { commit = true } }]

Track the manifest and a build-setting variable, whose changed value forces a rebuild.

[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { env = "MY_BUILD_SETTING" }]

The lab's content fingerprint

This lab uses cache-keys = [{ env = "CACHE_DEMO_KEY" }]. After generating the fixture, scripts/build_key.py hashes pyproject.toml, Python source, JSON, and bundled data. Supply its result to every sync that installs the local package. Identical content can reuse a wheel across fresh CI checkouts even when file timestamps differ. --no-editable installs that wheel instead of linking the source tree.

docs.title: Populate and Inspect the Cache
docs.text:
uv organizes cached data into distinct target types. These include Prebuilt Wheels downloaded from package indexes, Source-built Wheels built locally, and Unpacked Source Distributions used during builds. When enabled, Centralized Project Environments are also cached so a project can reuse its installed packages.

Downloaded wheelsLocally built wheelUnzipped source distributionCentralized project environmentOther Unused Cache Entries

Prebuilt Wheels are downloaded from package indexes and can be installed without building the package from source. uv caches them so later installs can reuse them instead of downloading them again.

Create an ignored directory for the disposable experiments in later tabs.

mkdir -p lab

Create the project environment for the following experiments.

uv venv --python 3.12

Install a small numerical-computing stack directly with uv pip install. --only-binary :all: selects prebuilt wheels when available.

uv pip install \
  --python .venv/bin/python \
  --only-binary :all: \
  numpy \
  scipy \
  matplotlib

Measure the populated cache; cache-size is a preview feature in this uv version.

uv cache size --human --preview-features cache-size

Source-built Wheels are built locally from source packages and stored in the cache. Reusing a cached wheel avoids repeating the build when its inputs have not changed.

Generate the deterministic 16 MiB fixture before building the local package.

.venv/bin/python scripts/generate_fixture.py

Install the project as a regular wheel; the content fingerprint determines when uv rebuilds it.

CACHE_DEMO_KEY=$(.venv/bin/python scripts/build_key.py) \
uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-editable \
  --python 3.12

Run the installed package and write a PNG report.

.venv/bin/python -m uv_cache_demo.main --output reports/embeddings.png

Locate the locally built wheel; its path is the checkpoint for later pruning.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f -name 'uv_cache_demo-*.whl' -print

Unpacked Source Distributions are extracted source trees that uv uses to build wheels. uv can cache both the unpacked source and the wheel produced from it.

Force a source build of small idna into an ignored target, without changing the project's lockfile.

uv pip install \
  --python "$(uv python find 3.12)" \
  --target lab/sdist-target \
  --no-deps \
  --no-binary idna \
  'idna==3.10'

Inspect source-cache buckets; their version suffixes are internal details and may change.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d -name 'sdists-v*' -print

Locate uv's unpacked idna source (src/idna) while it is still present.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d -path '*/sdists-v*/pypi/idna/3.10/*/src/idna' -print

Find the idna wheel built from that source, distinct from the downloaded numerical-library wheels.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f -name 'idna-*.whl' -print

Centralized Project Environments store a project's virtual environment in uv's central cache directory instead of alongside its pyproject.toml. The opt-in --centralized-project-envs preview feature connects .venv to the cached environment, usually with a link.

Create an ignored, disposable project to keep the main .venv separate.

mkdir -p lab/centralized

Copy the locked project declarations into that directory; the project itself will not be installed there.

cp pyproject.toml uv.lock lab/centralized/

Populate the cached environment without specifying UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT or --active: explicit environment paths bypass centralization.

uv --preview-features centralized-project-envs sync \
  --directory lab/centralized \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --python 3.12

Inspect the .venv link pointing into uv's cache (uv may use a path file if linking is unavailable).

ls -ld lab/centralized/.venv

Check that dependencies import from the new environment rather than the main project's .venv.

lab/centralized/.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy; print(numpy.__version__)'

Other Unused Cache Entries are classified by cache metadata and references, not installation status. An older uv may create cache entries in a format a newer version does not recognize; those entries can be removed while the installed package remains in .venv or --target. Unreferenced unpacked wheel archives may also be considered unused, but a current-format wheel is not unused just because its package is uninstalled.

Create a directory for the disposable package installs.

mkdir -p lab/prune-probe

Use uv 0.4.12 through uvx to install a prebuilt packaging wheel into an ignored target.

UV_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.cache/uvx-prune-bootstrap" \
  uvx --from 'uv==0.4.12' uv \
  --cache-dir "$(uv cache dir)" \
  pip install \
  --python "$(uv python find 3.12)" \
  --target lab/prune-probe/old-wheel \
  --reinstall \
  --no-deps \
  --only-binary packaging \
  'packaging==24.2'

Use the same old uv version to build a wheel from the idna source distribution.

UV_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.cache/uvx-prune-bootstrap" \
  uvx --from 'uv==0.4.12' uv \
  --cache-dir "$(uv cache dir)" \
  pip install \
  --python "$(uv python find 3.12)" \
  --target lab/prune-probe/old-sdist \
  --reinstall \
  --no-deps \
  --no-binary idna \
  'idna==3.10'

Inspect the cache buckets created by both the current and older uv versions; bucket names and versions are implementation details and may change.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d -printf '%f\n' | sort

docs.title: Offline Synchronization
docs.text:
Remove just the installed environment, leaving uv's cache available.

rm -rf .venv

Restore it without network access; the fixture and build fingerprint are still available.

CACHE_DEMO_KEY=$("$(uv python find 3.12)" scripts/build_key.py) \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-editable \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Confirm that NumPy and the local wheel import from .venv.

.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy, uv_cache_demo; print(numpy.__file__, uv_cache_demo.__file__)'

docs.title: Compare UV_LINK_MODE
docs.text:
Use four disposable environments to compare installation modes without changing the main .venv. Each tab synchronizes the locked dependencies into a separate environment; --offline ensures these trials reuse the cached wheels. On a bind-mounted workspace, hardlink or clone may fall back to copying if the cache and environment are on different filesystems.

CloneCopyHardlinkSymlink

Sync into a disposable environment with clone, uv's normal Linux/macOS mode. Where supported, the environment initially shares disk blocks with the cache, then gets separate blocks when files change. This can use less disk space than making full copies.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=lab/clone \
  UV_LINK_MODE=clone \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Inspect the installed file and its hard-link count; stat alone cannot prove whether copy-on-write cloning occurred.

stat -c '%F; hard links: %h' lab/clone/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py

Verify the installed NumPy version.

lab/clone/bin/python -c 'import numpy; print(numpy.__version__)'

Sync using copy to make independent files in the environment. This uses more disk space than shared-block modes, but changes to installed files do not change the cached files.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=lab/copy \
  UV_LINK_MODE=copy \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Inspect the installed file's type and link count.

stat -c '%F; hard links: %h' lab/copy/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py

Use hardlink to let the environment and cache share the same file on one filesystem, which saves disk space. Editing a hardlinked file also changes the cached file. If they are on different filesystems, uv falls back to making a copy.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=lab/hardlink \
  UV_LINK_MODE=hardlink \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Check whether the installed file has multiple hard links (%h greater than one).

stat -c '%F; hard links: %h' lab/hardlink/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py

Use symlink to make the environment's files point to files in the cache, avoiding separate copies. The environment depends on those cache paths, so cleaning or moving the cache can break it.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=lab/symlink \
  UV_LINK_MODE=symlink \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Inspect a link target to see why cleaning the cache would break this installation.

readlink lab/symlink/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py

Remove this disposable environment before the cleanup stages; retain the copy-mode .venv.

rm -rf lab/symlink

docs.title: Cache Cleanup Operations
docs.text:
uv provides different Cleanup Operations, each with its own rules for deciding what to remove from the cache. Depending on the command, cleanup may affect Prebuilt Wheels, Source-built Wheels, Unpacked Source Distributions, and Centralized Project Environments, as well as other Unused Cache Entries. The disk space reclaimed by each operation depends on the cache contents and artifact sizes, so a broader cleanup does not necessarily reclaim more space in a particular run.

Normal pruneCI pruneComplete Clean

The uv cache prune command performs the standard cleanup by removing Unused Cache Entries and all Centralized Project Environments. Unused entries may include Prebuilt Wheels, Unpacked Source Distributions, and Source-built Wheels. It retains entries that uv still considers in use, unlike uv cache clean, which removes every cache entry. Run the ordinary prune command:

uv cache prune

Confirm that the obsolete cache buckets created by uv 0.4.12 are gone. They contained the old packaging wheel and old idna built wheel.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -maxdepth 1 -type d \
  \( -name 'wheels-v1' -o -name 'built-wheels-v3' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the current prebuilt wheel entries for NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib remain.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d \
  \( -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/numpy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/scipy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/matplotlib' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the current-format wheels built from the local project and idna source remain.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f \
  \( -name 'uv_cache_demo-*.whl' -o -name 'idna-*.whl' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the unpacked idna source remains after ordinary pruning.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d \
  -path '*/sdists-v*/pypi/idna/3.10/*/src/idna' \
  -print

Confirm that pruning has not removed the packages installed into --target.

test -d lab/prune-probe/old-wheel/packaging
test -d lab/prune-probe/old-sdist/idna

Confirm the main, non-centralized .venv remains usable.

.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy; print(numpy.__version__)'

Measure the cache size after pruning.

uv cache size --human --preview-features cache-size

The uv cache prune --ci command is designed for CI environments. To support this strategy, it retains current-format Source-built Wheels, which can take significant time and computing resources to build and can save time in later CI runs. It removes Prebuilt Wheels and Unpacked Source Distributions to reduce cache size as those are generally quick to download again. The command also performs ordinary pruning, so it can remove obsolete source-built wheels. Run the CI-specific prune command:

uv cache prune --ci

Confirm that the obsolete cache buckets created by uv 0.4.12 are gone. They contained the old packaging wheel and old idna built wheel.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -maxdepth 1 -type d \
  \( -name 'wheels-v1' -o -name 'built-wheels-v3' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the prebuilt wheel entries for NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib are gone (no output expected).

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d \
  \( -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/numpy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/scipy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/matplotlib' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the current-format wheels built from the local project and idna source remain.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f \
  \( -name 'uv_cache_demo-*.whl' -o -name 'idna-*.whl' \) \
  -print

Check that the unzipped idna source is gone (no output expected).

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d -path '*/sdists-v*/pypi/idna/3.10/*/src/idna' -print

Verify the saved centralized environment target is gone; its .venv link may be dangling.

test ! -d "$(cat lab/centralized-target)"

Confirm that pruning has not removed the packages installed into --target.

test -d lab/prune-probe/old-wheel/packaging
test -d lab/prune-probe/old-sdist/idna

Measure the cache size after pruning.

uv cache size --human --preview-features cache-size

Confirm that installed packages in the main copy-mode .venv still import.

.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy; from uv_cache_demo.main import cache_message; print(cache_message())'

docs.title: Using uv's Cache in CI Environments
docs.text: Aggressive caching helps make uv fast by avoiding repeated downloads and builds of dependencies. In CI, however, transferring a cache between temporary Hosted Runners adds overhead, so preserving everything is not always worthwhile. Astral's CI caching guidance favors Wheels Built from Source, which can be costly to rebuild, over Prebuilt Wheels, which are usually quick to download and install. It does not cite a formal study quantifying these trade-offs; this section explains how to adopt the strategy and measure its benefits in your own GitHub Actions workflow. For Docker builds, see Using uv's Cache in Docker Builds.

docs.text:
This table lists the workflow and project files used in the examples.

Component Description .github/workflows/uv-cache.yml GitHub Actions workflow that compares cold, complete, and CI-pruned caches and records install time and local cache size. notebooks/nb5_uv_cache_lab/pyproject.toml and uv.lock Define the package build configuration and locked dependencies installed by the workflow.

docs.title: Using uv's Cache in GitHub Actions
GitHub Actions Remote Cache Service
docs.text:
GitHub Actions provides an Integrated Remote Cache Service for storing and restoring files across workflow runs; this is particularly useful for ephemeral (GitHub) Hosted Runners, where each job starts on a fresh machine. A typical workflow setup consists of three layers:

  1. The GitHub Actions Cache - Stores cache archives between workflow runs. Cache keys and GitHub's access rules determine which runs can restore an archive.
  2. The Package-Manager Cache - A local cache used by tools such as Python's uv, Rust's cargo, and Node.js's npm to reuse downloads and build artifacts. The CI service can archive and restore this local data between runs; it is not a second remote cache.
  3. The Project Environment - Contains dependencies installed for running the project's application and tests. Ephemeral runners typically create it fresh for each job; this workflow does not cache it.

docs.title: Cache Lifecycle on Temporary Runners
docs.text:
Persistent Runners are typically self-hosted GitHub Actions machines that remain available between jobs, allowing local data to persist. Temporary Runners, usually GitHub-hosted, start with a clean environment and are discarded after each job, including their local data. While persistent runners can reuse local caches, temporary runners rely on GitHub Actions' remote caching service to preserve and restore cached data across jobs. In both cases, remote caches are subject to GitHub's retention and eviction policies. Caches expire after seven days without access and may be evicted earlier when storage limits are reached (retention and eviction policies). A well-designed caching strategy is particularly important for temporary runners to balance storage costs, cache transfer overhead, and overall job duration.

Astral's uv provides a sophisticated caching approach with several strategies:

  • Warm Caching: Restore the complete existing cache before dependency installation and reuse all cached packages and build artifacts. Unlike CI-pruned caching, retain all cache contents when saving it for subsequent runs.
  • Cold Caching: Skip cache restoration and saving, forcing dependencies to be downloaded or built again. Useful as a baseline for measuring caching benefits.
  • CI-Pruned Caching: Restore the cache while removing downloaded Pre-Built Wheels and Unpacked Source Distributions before saving. Retain Source-Built Wheels to reduce cache size while preserving potentially expensive build artifacts.

docs.title: Analysis Job and Steps
docs.text:
The analyze-embeddings job checks out the repository and sets up Python 3.12. The fixture_size choice selects a 16, 64, 256, 512, or 1024 MiB synthetic embedding matrix, defaulting to 256 MiB. The job generates the matrix, fingerprints the project's build inputs, and installs uv with optional package-cache restoration. After recording the pre-install cache size, it creates a fresh environment from the lockfile and times uv sync. Finally, it analyzes the installed embeddings and summarizes the selected size, cache sizes, restoration status, and installation time. The YAML below shows the workflow trigger and job configuration.

name: uv cache demo

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      strategy:
        description: "uv cache strategy"
        type: choice
        default: ci-pruned
        options:
          - cold
          - warm
          - ci-pruned
      fixture_size:
        description: "Embedding matrix size (MiB)"
        type: choice
        default: "256"
        options:
          - "16"
          - "64"
          - "256"
          - "512"
          - "1024"

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  analyze-embeddings:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      CACHE_STRATEGY: ${{ inputs.strategy || 'ci-pruned' }}
      fixture_size: ${{ inputs.fixture_size || '256' }}

docs.title: Step: Set up uv and Optionally Restore its Package Cache
docs.text:
The astral-sh/setup-uv GitHub Action is developed, released, and maintained by Astral, the company behind uv. It installs uv, adds it to the runner's PATH, and provides options to configure its setup and package-cache behavior, including cache restoration, pruning, and saving. Its remote cache key incorporates an internal cache version, architecture, platform, and detected Python version, along with a hash of matching files; the explicit patterns in this workflow cover dependencies and local build inputs, including generated data, so changes invalidate the remote cache.

After a successful job, the post-action of astral-sh/setup-uv saves the remote cache when needed. An exact key hit skips pruning and saving; otherwise, the ci-pruned strategy runs uv cache prune --ci before saving, while warm saves without pruning. Because GitHub cache entries are immutable, the action creates a new entry instead of overwriting one. Cold experiments disable saving.

- name: Set up uv and optionally restore its package cache
  id: uv
  uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@07a047e608db84b3d8c06cd9a7c7dcc9c355c18e # v10.3.2
  with:
    version: "0.11.1"
    enable-cache: true
    restore-cache: ${{ env.CACHE_STRATEGY != 'cold' }}
    save-cache: ${{ env.CACHE_STRATEGY == 'cold' && 'false' || 'auto' }}
    prune-cache: ${{ env.CACHE_STRATEGY == 'ci-pruned' }}
    cache-suffix: ${{ env.CACHE_STRATEGY == 'warm' && 'full-cache-demo' || '' }}
    cache-dependency-glob: |
      notebooks/nb5_uv_cache_lab/pyproject.toml
      notebooks/nb5_uv_cache_lab/uv.lock
      notebooks/nb5_uv_cache_lab/scripts/*.py
      notebooks/nb5_uv_cache_lab/src/**/*.py
      notebooks/nb5_uv_cache_lab/src/**/*.json
      notebooks/nb5_uv_cache_lab/src/**/*.bin

Inputs: (excerpt)

  • enable-cache - Explicitly enables GitHub Actions caching; its auto default enables caching on GitHub-hosted runners for supported events.
  • restore-cache - Restores matching artifacts for warm and ci-pruned. Selecting cold disables restoration, giving a cold installation without uv cache clean. This relies on fresh hosted runners. The action defaults to "true".
  • save-cache - Uses "auto" during normal runs and "false" during cold experiments, leaving remote archives unchanged. The "auto" default allows eligible saving except for merge_group events; it does not make installation cold.
  • prune-cache - Enables uv cache prune --ci before a new cache is saved after a cache miss for the ci-pruned strategy; in v10.3.2, the default is false.
  • cache-suffix - Separates the warm complete cache from the CI-pruned cache.
  • cache-dependency-glob - Replaces the default lockfile and requirements patterns with the listed repository-relative paths, which are used to generate the remote cache key.

Outputs: (excerpt)

  • cache-hit - Indicates whether restoration found an archive. When restoration is disabled, v10.3.2 leaves this output unset, so the summary explicitly reports Skipped.
CI-pruned CacheWarm CacheCold Cache

Restore the CI-pruned cache and save it automatically on a miss. Pruning removes downloaded prebuilt wheels before saving while retaining current source-built wheels; the suffix is empty.

with:
  enable-cache: true
  restore-cache: true
  save-cache: auto
  prune-cache: true
  cache-suffix: ""

Restore and save the complete cache without pruning. The suffix separates it from the CI-pruned cache.

with:
  enable-cache: true
  restore-cache: true
  save-cache: auto
  prune-cache: false
  cache-suffix: full-cache-demo

Keep caching enabled for consistent action setup and cache-key calculation, but skip restoration and saving. On a fresh runner, uv starts with an empty local cache and populates it during the job; remote archives remain unchanged. Pruning and the suffix do not affect this run.

with:
  enable-cache: true
  restore-cache: false
  save-cache: false
  prune-cache: false
  cache-suffix: ""

For warm and ci-pruned, a cache miss can populate an archive for a later run. Only a run reporting Restored qualifies as a warm measurement; check the uv sync log as well to confirm that the project wheel was reused.

docs.title: Step: Measure Restored Package Cache Size
docs.text:
Before installing dependencies, the workflow measures the package cache available on the runner so the report shows what was ready for reuse. It records the size in bytes and a readable unit such as MiB or GiB. It then exposes both values through GITHUB_ENV so the final step can reuse them.

- name: Measure restored package cache size
  run: |
    mkdir -p "$UV_CACHE_DIR"
    bytes=$(du -sb "$UV_CACHE_DIR" | cut -f1)
    echo "RESTORED_CACHE_BYTES=$bytes" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
    echo "RESTORED_CACHE_SIZE=$(numfmt --to=iec-i --suffix=B "$bytes")" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

docs.title: Step: Create a Fresh Environment from Locked Dependencies
docs.text:
As explained above, GitHub Actions can restore a remote package cache on a fresh (Github-) Hosted Runner and save cache updates after a run. Additionally, uv supports project-specific cache keys, that can be defined as tool.uv.cache-keys in pyproject.toml to fingerprint local wheel-cache entries, complementing the remote cache key.

[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ env = "CACHE_DEMO_KEY" }]

Earlier, the workflow generates a synthetic embedding matrix of the selected size (256 MiB by default) and exposes a fingerprint of the build inputs as CACHE_DEMO_KEY. With Python 3.12, uv sync creates the .venv and uses --locked to follow the committed uv.lock (and fail if it needs updating). The --no-editable option installs a regular project wheel containing the matrix rather than linking the source; the fingerprint lets uv reuse a cached wheel or rebuild it when inputs change. The step exposes the uv sync duration in milliseconds as milliseconds through GitHub Outputs, excluding fixture generation, cache transfers, pruning, and report execution.

- name: Create a fresh environment from locked dependencies
  id: install
  shell: bash
  run: |
    start_ms=$(date +%s%3N)
    uv sync \
      --directory notebooks/nb5_uv_cache_lab \
      --locked \
      --no-editable \
      --python 3.12
    end_ms=$(date +%s%3N)
    echo "milliseconds=$((end_ms - start_ms))" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

docs.title: Step: Show Cache and Installation Time
docs.text:
The final job summary shows the selected strategy, whether a cache was restored, the cache sizes before and after installation, and the installation time. The previous step recorded the install duration of uv sync in milliseconds and exposed the value as milliseconds output, which the summary uses as INSTALL_MS. Cache sizes are measured on the (GitHub-) Hosted Runner, not from compressed remote archives; if restoration is skipped or misses, the pre-install size does not represent a restored cache.

- name: Show cache and installation time
  env:
    RESTORE_STATUS: ${{ env.CACHE_STRATEGY == 'cold' && 'Skipped' || (steps.uv.outputs.cache-hit == 'true' && 'Restored' || 'Not restored') }}
    INSTALL_MS: ${{ steps.install.outputs.milliseconds }}
  run: |
    cache_bytes=$(du -sb "$UV_CACHE_DIR" | cut -f1)
    cache_size=$(numfmt --to=iec-i --suffix=B "$cache_bytes")
    echo "RESTORED_CACHE_SIZE=$RESTORED_CACHE_SIZE ($RESTORED_CACHE_BYTES bytes)"
    echo "CACHE_SIZE_AFTER_SYNC=$cache_size ($cache_bytes bytes; before setup-uv post-action pruning)"
    {
      echo '## uv cache demo'
      echo ''
      echo '| Measurement | Result |'
      echo '| --- | --- |'
      echo "| Embedding matrix size | ${fixture_size} MiB |"
      echo "| setup-uv cache restoration | $RESTORE_STATUS |"
      echo "| Cache strategy | $CACHE_STRATEGY |"
      echo "| Restored local uv cache | $RESTORED_CACHE_SIZE |"
      echo "| uv sync duration | ${INSTALL_MS} ms |"
      echo "| Local uv cache after sync, before post-action pruning | $cache_size |"
      echo ''
      echo 'Duration measures only uv sync; it excludes GitHub cache restoration and saving time.'
      echo 'Cold experiments skip cache restoration and saving; remote archives remain unchanged.'
      echo 'Only runs reporting Restored qualify as warm-cache measurements.'
      echo 'Compare multiple runs with unchanged dependencies and build inputs; no speedup is guaranteed.'
    } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

docs.title: Run the Workflow and Compare Cache Performance
Execute the Cache Strategy Comparison
docs.text:
To test uv's recommendation for caching in CI, the workflow was executed with different caching strategies and embedding-matrix sizes. The comparison examined whether retaining only costly source-built wheels could reduce cache size and overall job duration compared with keeping the complete cache or starting without one. The following conditions were varied:

  • Caching strategy: The setup-uv input prune-cache controlled which artifacts were saved: true retained costly Source-built Wheels but removed Downloaded Prebuilt Wheels for the CI-pruned Cache, while false retained both for the Warm (complete) cache. The Cold (empty) cache baseline used restore-cache: false and save-cache: false on a fresh runner, skipping restoration and leaving remote archives unchanged.
  • Source-built wheel share: Packaging matrices from 16 to 1,024 MiB into the source-built wheel changed its contribution to the overall cache. Each size used a distinct cache key; larger matrices also increased generation and analysis time.

The following table shows the runs for each estimated source-built wheel share and caching strategy, for 45 measurements in total. Each combination was run three times because timings can vary; the middle result (the median) helps reduce the influence of an unusually fast or slow run.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The experiment described above ran on GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runners using Python 3.12 and uv 0.11.1. Results and links to the individual runs were gathered in the benchmark CSV. It records median durations from three successful runs per workload and strategy; total job time includes cache transfers and other workflow steps, while uv sync time measures installation alone.

The graph compares all three caching strategies. Its x-axis shows the median restored CI-pruned cache size as a percentage of the median restored complete cache size, an estimate of the source-built wheel's contribution rather than the matrix's exact share. The same reference percentage applies to every strategy for a given workload. The y-axis shows total job duration in seconds, including post-actions but excluding queue time; lower values mean faster jobs. Lines connect the medians, and error bars show the minimum and maximum durations across the three measured runs.

docs.title: Key Findings and Conclusions
docs.text:
These results illustrate the trade-offs described in Astral's CI caching guidance. A larger cache can accelerate dependency installation, but its transfer overhead may outweigh the savings in total job duration.

  • Cache strategy matters: The CI-pruned cache delivered the shortest median job duration in most larger workload scenarios, while the complete cache consistently provided the fastest uv sync.
  • Cache size vs. performance: The complete cache restored substantially more data (up to 2,461 MiB), but faster dependency installation did not necessarily translate into faster overall jobs.
  • Workload dependency: The complete cache was competitive at smaller estimated shares, where measurement ranges often overlapped. At the two largest estimated shares, the CI-pruned cache delivered the shortest median job duration.
  • Cache validation: A restored archive did not always prevent a project rebuild. Stale caches were refreshed, and warm runs that rebuilt the project were excluded from the comparison.
  • Measurement limitations: Each scenario includes only three runs. Runner performance, cache transfer, and workload execution introduce variability.

Overall conclusion: These findings provide a useful indication of how cache strategies can affect CI performance, but they are specific to this project, its dependencies, and the tested GitHub Actions environment. They should not be generalized into a universal ranking. Validate the results against your own workload before choosing a caching strategy.

Note: Warm-cache measurements reused existing archives without saving new ones; the cold baseline skipped both cache restoration and saving.

docs.title: Connecting Grafana to InfluxDB
docs.text: The license service records API requests in InfluxDB. Each request is stored in the api_requests measurement with the HTTP method, endpoint, and response status code.

docs.title: Open Grafana
docs.text:
Start the monitoring stack with Docker Compose and open Grafana:

http://localhost:3001

Log in with the Grafana administrator credentials configured in the .env file:

  • Username: admin
  • Password: admin1234

docs.title: Add InfluxDB as a data source
docs.text:
In Grafana, open Connections → Data sources → Add new data source and select InfluxDB.

Use these settings:

  • Query language: Flux
  • URL: http://influxdb:8086
  • Organization: oidc_license_service
  • Default bucket: api_metrics
  • Token: the value of INFLUXDB_TOKEN from .env

Use http://influxdb:8086 rather than http://localhost:8086. Grafana runs inside Docker, so localhost refers to the Grafana container. The name influxdb resolves to the InfluxDB service on the Docker network.

Click Save & test. Grafana should confirm that the data source is working.

docs.title: Query API metrics
docs.text:
Create a dashboard and add a panel using the InfluxDB data source. A basic Flux query for recent API calls is:

from(bucket: "api_metrics")
    |> range(start: -1h)
    |> filter(fn: (r) => r._measurement == "api_requests")

The stored data contains:

  • method — the HTTP method, such as GET or POST.
  • endpoint — the requested API path.
  • _field — normally status_code.
  • _value — the HTTP response status code.

The middleware writes the metric after the request completes. Successful writes return no value; InfluxDB raises an exception when a synchronous write fails. Monitoring errors are logged and do not cause an otherwise healthy API request to fail.

docs.title: Count API calls over time
docs.text:
To create a dashboard panel that displays the number of API calls over time:

  1. Open Dashboards → New → New dashboard.
  2. Click Add visualization.
  3. Select the InfluxDB data source.
  4. Switch to Code mode and enter this Flux query:
from(bucket: "api_metrics")
    |> range(start: v.timeRangeStart, stop: v.timeRangeStop)
    |> filter(fn: (r) => r._measurement == "api_requests")
    |> filter(fn: (r) => r._field == "status_code")
    |> aggregateWindow(every: 1m, fn: count, createEmpty: true)
    |> yield(name: "api_calls")
  1. Select the Time series visualization.
  2. Set the panel title to API Calls Over Time.
  3. Click Apply and save the dashboard.

The query counts the status_code field once for every recorded request and groups the results into one-minute intervals. The dashboard time-range selector controls which requests are included.

For a single total count, create a Stat visualization with this query:

from(bucket: "api_metrics")
    |> range(start: v.timeRangeStart, stop: v.timeRangeStop)
    |> filter(fn: (r) => r._measurement == "api_requests")
    |> filter(fn: (r) => r._field == "status_code")
    |> count()

docs.title: Show requester IPs and endpoints in a table
docs.text:
To list one row for each API request with its timestamp, requester IP, endpoint, and response status code:

  1. Add a new Grafana panel.
  2. Select the InfluxDB data source.
  3. Switch to Code mode.
  4. Use this Flux query:
from(bucket: "api_metrics")
    |> range(start: v.timeRangeStart, stop: v.timeRangeStop)
    |> filter(fn: (r) => r._measurement == "api_requests")
    |> filter(fn: (r) => r._field == "status_code")
    |> group()
    |> keep(columns: ["_time", "client_ip", "endpoint", "_value"])
    |> rename(columns: {
        _time: "Time",
        client_ip: "Requester",
        endpoint: "Endpoint",
        _value: "StatusCode",
    })
    |> sort(columns: ["Time"], desc: true)
  1. Set the query result format to Table in the query editor. Do not use Time series format, because Grafana displays tags as series labels in that mode.
  2. Select the Table visualization.
  3. In the table options, disable Column filter to remove the filter row at the bottom of the table.
  4. Set the panel title to API Calls by Requester.
  5. Apply and save the panel.

The resulting table contains one line per recorded request with these columns:

  • Time — when the request was recorded.
  • Requester — the requester IP address.
  • Endpoint — the requested API path.
  • StatusCode — the HTTP response status code.

The group() call combines the individual InfluxDB series into one table so the tags remain normal columns instead of being rendered as a series label. This query does not use count() or pivot(), so requests are not grouped or aggregated. Each InfluxDB point remains a separate table row.

If the table does not update after adding the client_ip tag, restart the backend container and generate new requests. Existing InfluxDB points do not contain tags that were added later.

docs.title: Applied Project
docs.text:
The applied project is an integrated license service for issuing and validating Cloudsmith credentials. It consists of three main application components:

  • A Streamlit frontend provides the browser-based user interface. Users sign in through the frontend and can retrieve or validate their license.
  • A Keycloak provides the OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity service. It authenticates users, manages the configured realm and client, and issues tokens for authenticated requests.
  • A FastAPI backend validates OIDC access tokens, authorizes protected operations, stores license data in SQLite, and integrates with Cloudsmith.
  • The PyGuard library provides brute-force protection middleware for the backend. It tracks requests to protected endpoints and can temporarily block clients that exceed the configured attempt threshold.

    F --> K["Keycloak OIDC"]
    K -->|access token| F
    F -->|Bearer token| A["FastAPI backend"]
    A -->|create or refresh license| C["Cloudsmith API"]
    A --> D["SQLite license database"]

For more information

The individual components are documented in their own README files:

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
Docker Compose starts the frontend, backend, and Keycloak services and places them on a shared network. The project demonstrates how a user-facing application, an external identity provider, a protected API, local persistence, and a third-party license service work together as one deployable system.

The Compose configuration is stored in projects/bonus1_license_service_oidc/docker-compose.yml. 

services:
  devcontainer:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: .devcontainer/Dockerfile
    command: sleep infinity
    depends_on:
      - backend
      - frontend
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace:cached
    working_dir: /workspace
    networks:
      license_service_network:

  backend:
    build:
      context: ./backend
      additional_contexts:
        pyguard: ../proj1_pyguard
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - license_service_data:/app/data
    env_file:
      - .env
    environment:
      ADMIN_API_KEY: ${ADMIN_API_KEY:-dev-secret}
      OIDC_ISSUER_URL: http://keycloak.localhost:8081/realms/license-service
      OIDC_JWKS_URL: http://keycloak:8080/realms/license-service/protocol/openid-connect/certs
      DATABASE_PATH: /app/data/licenses.db
    networks:
      license_service_network:
        ipv4_address: ${BACKEND_IP:-172.30.0.2}

  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    depends_on:
      - backend
    ports:
      - "8501:8501"
    extra_hosts:
      - "keycloak.localhost:172.30.0.1"
    volumes:
      - ./frontend/.streamlit/secrets.toml:/run/secrets/streamlit-secrets.toml:ro
    networks:
      license_service_network:
        ipv4_address: ${FRONTEND_IP:-172.30.0.3}
    environment:
      BACKEND_URL: http://backend:8080
      ADMIN_API_KEY: ${ADMIN_API_KEY:-dev-secret}

  keycloak:
    image: quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.3
    command: start-dev --import-realm
    environment:
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME: ${KEYCLOAK_ADMIN:-admin}
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin}
      KC_HOSTNAME: http://keycloak.localhost:8081
    ports:
      - "8081:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./keycloak/realm-export.json:/opt/keycloak/data/import/realm-export.json:ro
    networks:
      license_service_network:
        ipv4_address: ${KEYCLOAK_IP:-172.30.0.4}

networks:
  license_service_network:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.30.0.0/24

volumes:
  license_service_data:

The most important Compose configuration keys are:

Key Purpose services Defines the containers that make up the application. build Builds a service image from a local Dockerfile. depends_on Defines service startup order. ports Maps host ports to container ports. environment Passes configuration values into a container. volumes Mounts the Keycloak realm and Streamlit secrets. networks Connects services to a shared Docker network. ipam and subnet Configure the address range of that network.

The project-level .env file supplies variable values used by Docker Compose. Compose loads these values when it reads the file and substitutes them into ${...} expressions in docker-compose.yml, while each service's env_file setting passes the selected variables into that container's environment.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Each entry under services describes one container role. Compose also gives each service a network identity that other services can use.

The backend service exposes port 8080, the frontend service exposes port 8501, and Keycloak exposes port 8081 to the host. The frontend declares a dependency on the backend so Compose starts the backend first. The Keycloak service imports the realm definition from keycloak/realm-export.json.

depends_on expresses startup order, but it does not prove that a dependency is ready to accept requests. Applications that need readiness guarantees should use health checks, retries, or an explicit readiness check.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
The frontend, backend, and Keycloak services join the license_service_network network. The network uses the 172.30.0.0/24 subnet, with configurable addresses for the services.

Published ports are different from internal service addresses. Port 8501 makes the frontend available to the host, while port 8080 makes the backend available to the host. Container-to-container traffic uses service names on the internal Compose network.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Compose provides internal DNS-based service discovery. A container can resolve another service using the service name from the Compose file:

http://backend:8080
http://keycloak:8080

This is more stable than hard-coding an IP address because containers may be recreated and receive different private addresses.

docs.title: Applied Project
docs.text:
Section 02 extends the project introduced in Section 01 with a monitoring stack for API metrics and backend logs.

The monitoring stack consists of these components:

  • InfluxDB stores the API metrics as time-series data.
  • Grafana visualizes the metrics in dashboards.
  • Grafana Alloy collects backend container logs and forwards them to Loki.
  • Loki stores the logs for querying and visualization in Grafana.
flowchart LR
    B["Browser"] --> F["Streamlit frontend"]
    F --> K["Keycloak OIDC"]
    K --> F
    F --> A["FastAPI backend"]
    A --> GUARD["..."]
    subgraph MIDDLEWARE["Middleware"]
      GUARD --> METRICS["InfluxDB metrics"]
    end
    METRICS --> INFLUXDB["InfluxDB"]
    INFLUXDB --> GRAFANA["Grafana"]

    ALLOY --> LOKI["Loki"]

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
The Compose setup includes the monitoring services shown below:

services:

  loki:
    image: grafana/loki:3.4.2
    command: -config.file=/etc/loki/config.yaml
    volumes:
      - ./logging/loki/config.yaml:/etc/loki/config.yaml:ro
      - loki_data:/loki
    networks:
      - license_service_network

  alloy:
    image: grafana/alloy:v1.8.3
    command:
      - run
      - --server.http.listen-addr=0.0.0.0:12345
      - --storage.path=/var/lib/alloy/data
      - /etc/alloy/config.alloy
    depends_on:
      - loki
    volumes:
      - ./logging/alloy/config.alloy:/etc/alloy/config.alloy:ro
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
      - alloy_data:/var/lib/alloy/data
    networks:
      - license_service_network

  influxdb:
    image: influxdb:2.7
    container_name: influxdb
    env_file:
      - .env
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8086/ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s

    networks:
      license_service_network:
        ipv4_address: ${INFLUXDB_IP:-172.30.0.40}
    ports:
      - "8086:8086"
    volumes:
      - influxdb_data:/var/lib/influxdb2

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:10.4.0
    container_name: grafana
    env_file:
      - .env
    depends_on:
      influxdb:
        condition: service_healthy
      loki:
        condition: service_started
    networks:
      license_service_network:
        ipv4_address: ${GRAFANA_IP:-172.30.0.50}
    ports:
      - "3001:3000"
    volumes:
      - grafana_data:/var/lib/grafana

networks:
  license_service_network:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.30.0.0/24

volumes:
  license_service_data:
  influxdb_data:
  grafana_data:
  loki_data:
  alloy_data:

Compared to the previous section, the most important monitoring-related differences are:

Key Purpose influxdb service Runs InfluxDB 2.7 as the time-series database for API metrics. grafana service Runs Grafana and provides dashboards for the metrics stored in InfluxDB. loki service Stores backend container logs; configure Grafana's Loki data source with URL http://loki:3100. alloy service Collects backend container logs from Docker and forwards them to Loki. docker.sock Docker socket mount Lets Alloy discover and read container logs; it grants powerful Docker access, so use only in a trusted environment. healthcheck Checks the InfluxDB /ping endpoint so Grafana starts only after InfluxDB is ready. influxdb_data Persists InfluxDB data when the container is recreated. grafana_data Persists Grafana dashboards, users, and data-source configuration. loki_data and alloy_data Persist Loki's log data and Alloy's collection state across container recreation.

docs.title: InfluxDB
docs.text:
Integrating the influx client in the middleware

The backend writes each incoming request through its middleware stack to the Influx database. Therefore, it uses one measurement, api_requests, for all requests. It records method, endpoint, and client_ip as tags, and status_code and duration_ms as fields. Duration is measured in milliseconds around request handling. The Point constructor from influxdb-client is used to create each InfluxDB record:

# middleware.py
import os

from influxdb_client import InfluxDBClient, Point
from influxdb_client.client.write_api import SYNCHRONOUS

client = InfluxDBClient(
    url=os.getenv("INFLUXDB_URL"),
    token=os.environ["INFLUXDB_TOKEN"],
    org=os.getenv("INFLUXDB_ORG"),
)
write_api = client.write_api(write_options=SYNCHRONOUS)

point = (
  Point("api_requests")
    .tag("method", method)
    .tag("endpoint", endpoint)
    .tag("client_ip", client_ip)
    .field("duration_ms", duration_ms)
    .field("status_code", status_code)
)

write_api.write( bucket=os.environ["INFLUXDB_BUCKET"], org=os.environ["INFLUXDB_ORG"], record=point, )

Exploring metrics in influx

Open http://localhost:8086 in your browser and sign in with the InfluxDB credentials from the .env file. Open Data Explorer and select the api_metrics buckets.

Data Explorer lets you explore the data stored in InfluxDB without building a dashboard first. You can choose a time range, focus on particular metrics, and display the results as a graph or table. Within the Data Explorer you can choose between the visual query builder or switch to Script Editor to enter a query directly.

api counts per minute

For a first example, select Script Editor and paste the following query. It uses Flux, InfluxDB's query language, to count API requests in one-minute intervals. Choose a time range that includes recent requests, then click Submit. If no data appears, send a few requests through the application and run the query again:

from(bucket: "api_metrics")
  |> range(start: v.timeRangeStart, stop: v.timeRangeStop)
  |> filter(fn: (r) => r._measurement == "api_requests")
  |> filter(fn: (r) => r._field == "status_code")
  |> aggregateWindow(every: 1m, fn: count, createEmpty: true)
  |> yield(name: "api_calls")
  • aggregateWindow counts the records in each one-minute interval and includes empty intervals with a count of zero.
  • yield names the result api_calls

docs.title: Grafana
docs.text:
Grafana is used as an visualization layer for the tracked metrics information and must be configured with the InfluxDB data source.

Open http://localhost:3001 in your browser and sign with the Grafana credentials from the .env file.

Connect Grafana with the Influx Database

To forward the metrics to Grafana, the Influx database has to be actively connected with the Grafana instance. Open Connections > Add new data source. Select InfluxDB and set Flux as the query language and use the following settings and confirm the with clicking on Save & test:

* URL: `http://influxdb:8086`
* Organization: `oidc_license_service`
* Bucket: `api_metrics`
* Token: `INFLUXDB_TOKEN` from `.env`

Exploring metrics with Grafana

Once the influx database is connected, navigate to Explore, set influxdb as the query language and provide the query from above into the code editor and run the query. The result should be the same as explored within InfluxDB.

Configuring Dashboards and alerts

Grafana provides the possibility to visualize metrics in configurable dashboards or configuring alerts when certain kind of thresholds are activated. Check the README of the grafana folder that provides detailed information about the used visualizations of the course:

  • a table view that lists incoming HTTP requests
  • a visualization showing HTTP traffic over time
  • a visualization showing average request latency over time
  • an alert for brute-force blocks, based on HTTP 429 responses

For more information

The individual dashboard and alert configuration are documented in the README

docs.title: Alloy
docs.text:
Grafana Alloy is an agent that collects telemetry and sends it to storage systems. Here it reads the backend's Docker logs and forwards them to Loki.

Docker socket mount

Compose mounts /var/run/docker.sock into Alloy so it can discover containers and read their logs. The :ro mount does not limit Docker API permissions, so access to this socket is powerful and should be restricted to trusted setups.

Log pipeline in config.alloy

The pipeline starts by discovering containers through Docker and keeping only the Compose service named backend:

discovery.docker "containers" {
  host = "unix:///var/run/docker.sock"
}

discovery.relabel "backend" {
  targets = discovery.docker.containers.targets

  rule {
    source_labels = ["__meta_docker_container_label_com_docker_compose_service"]
    regex         = "backend"
    action        = "keep"
  }
}

loki.source.docker reads logs from the matching containers and forwards them to loki.write, which sends them to Loki:

loki.source.docker "backend" {
  host       = "unix:///var/run/docker.sock"
  targets    = discovery.relabel.backend.output
  labels     = { job = "docker/backend" }
  forward_to = [loki.write.local.receiver]
}

loki.write "local" {
  endpoint {
    url = "http://loki:3100/loki/api/v1/push"
  }
}

The relabel rules also add service and container labels, which make backend logs easier to filter in Grafana.

docs.title: Loki
docs.text:
Loki is a log storage system. Alloy sends backend logs to Loki, where Grafana can query and display them.

Connect Grafana with Loki

In Grafana, open Connections > Add new data source, select Loki, and enter http://loki:3100 as the URL. Select Save & test. This service name works because Grafana and Loki share the Compose network.

Key settings in config.yaml

Loki listens on port 3100 and stores its data under /loki using the filesystem:

server:
  http_listen_port: 3100

common:
  path_prefix: /loki
  storage:
    filesystem:
      chunks_directory: /loki/chunks
      rules_directory: /loki/rules

The schema describes how Loki indexes stored logs. The compactor applies the configured retention period of 720h (30 days):

schema_config:
  configs:
    - store: tsdb
      from: "2024-01-01"
      object_store: filesystem
      schema: v13
      index:
        prefix: index_
        period: 24h

compactor:
  working_directory: /loki/compactor
  retention_enabled: true
  delete_request_store: filesystem

limits_config:
  retention_period: 720h

Authentication is disabled in this development configuration, so keep Loki on the trusted Compose network and do not expose it publicly.

This section uses Playwright and Artillery, both JavaScript-based tools. Rather than covering them in depth, it focuses on the infrastructure and setup needed to integrate them into the development and testing workflow.

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
docker-compose.yaml

The compose setup is extended with the new service devcontainer which provides the needed tools for our end-to-end testing chain. 

services:
  devcontainer:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: .devcontainer/Dockerfile
    command: sleep infinity
    depends_on:
      - backend
      - frontend
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace:cached
    working_dir: /workspace
    networks:
      license_service_network:

    ...

Dockerfile

The Dev Container image is based on Microsoft's JavaScript and Node.js development image and is stored in the required .devcontainer/Dockerfile path. It installs the command-line tools required by the project, including Bun, Playwright, and Artillery, and stores Playwright's browser binaries in a shared directory.

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/javascript-node:24-bookworm

SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]

ARG HTTP_PROXY
ARG HTTPS_PROXY
ARG NO_PROXY
ENV HTTP_PROXY=${HTTP_PROXY}
ENV HTTPS_PROXY=${HTTPS_PROXY}
ENV NO_PROXY=${NO_PROXY}
ENV PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/ms-playwright

USER root
RUN apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y \
    && apt-get install -y bats bats-support bats-assert bats-file dnsutils \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN curl -kfsSL https://bun.com/install \
    | sed 's/curl --fail/curl --insecure --fail/' \
    | bash \
    && cp /root/.bun/bin/bun /usr/local/bin/bun \
    && cp /root/.bun/bin/bunx /usr/local/bin/bunx

RUN mkdir -p /ms-playwright \
    && npm install -g @playwright/test@1.58.0 artillery \
    && apt-get update \
    && npx playwright install --with-deps \
    && chown -R node:node /ms-playwright

USER node
WORKDIR /workspace
ENV PATH=/workspace/node_modules/.bin:$PATH

EXPOSE 9323
CMD ["sleep", "infinity"]

bats-core

Bats-core is a Bash-based testing framework for writing and running automated tests. It is installed in the Dockerfile, but its use is outside the scope of this section.

The devcontainer.json file connects the development container to the existing Docker Compose application. It selects the devcontainer service and starts the other services alongside it, installs the relevant VS Code extensions, and forwards the application ports to the host.

  "runServices": [
    "backend",

    "devcontainer",
    "keycloak",
    "influxdb",
    "grafana"
  ],
  "customizations": {
    "vscode": {
      "extensions": [
        "ms-azuretools.vscode-docker",
        "ms-playwright.playwright"
      ]
    }
  },
  "forwardPorts": [
    8080,
    8501,
    8081,
    8086,
    3001
  ],
  "portsAttributes": {
    "8080": {
      "label": "Backend",
      "onAutoForward": "silent"
    },
    "8501": {

      "onAutoForward": "silent"
    },
    "8081": {
      "label": "Keycloak",
      "onAutoForward": "silent"
    },
    "8086": {
      "label": "InfluxDB",
      "onAutoForward": "silent"

docs.title: Playwright
docs.text:
Playwright is an end-to-end testing framework for automating browsers and verifying web applications from a user's perspective. It supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through one consistent API.

All browser-testing tools are provided inside the Dev Container: its Dockerfile installs Bun and bunx (L34-L38), then Playwright, Artillery, browser binaries, and required system dependencies (L41-L46).

The project's browser test verifies the OIDC login flow: it opens Streamlit, follows the redirect to Keycloak, signs in, and checks the authenticated UI.

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('signs in through Keycloak', async ({ page }) => {
  const username = process.env.KEYCLOAK_TEST_USERNAME;
  const password = process.env.KEYCLOAK_TEST_PASSWORD;

  if (!username || !password) {
    throw new Error('Set KEYCLOAK_TEST_USERNAME and KEYCLOAK_TEST_PASSWORD in .env');
  }

  await page.goto('/');
  await expect(page.getByText('🔑 License Service')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText('You are not logged in.')).toBeVisible();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in with Keycloak' }).click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL(
    /keycloak\.localhost:8081\/realms\/license-service\/protocol\/openid-connect\/auth/,
  );
  await page.locator('#username').fill(username);
  await page.locator('#password').fill(password);
  await page.locator('#kc-login').click();

  await expect(page.getByText(`Signed in as: ${username}`)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Get license' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'License Key' })).toBeVisible();
});

The page fixture provides an isolated browser page. page.goto('/') uses the frontend base URL from the Playwright configuration. Compose supplies the test credentials through environment variables; missing credentials fail the test immediately. After Keycloak redirects back to Streamlit, the assertions verify the username and license controls—not license creation or validation.

Playwright

See the README for more details about Playwright and the project configuration.

docs.title: Artillery
docs.text:
Artillery is a load-testing tool for measuring how an application behaves when it receives requests from many concurrent users. It helps identify performance bottlenecks, high error rates, and slow response times before they affect users in production.

Artillery tests are commonly configured in YAML. The config section sets the target service and load phases, while scenarios define the requests each virtual user makes. This test also uses the processor section to load custom JavaScript callbacks from helpers/test-helpers.cjs; these callbacks inspect responses, capture a returned license token, and validate it:

config:
  target: "http://backend:8080"

  phases:
    - duration: 60
      arrivalCount: 120
      name: "GET license brute-force limit"

  processor: "./helpers/test-helpers.cjs"

scenarios:
  - name: "GET license and validate returned token"
    flow:
      - get:
          url: "/licenses"
          headers:
            x-api-key: "dev-secret"
          afterResponse: "checkResponse"
      - ifTrue:
          condition: "{{ tokenCaptured }}"
          then:
            - get:
                url: "/licenses/{{ cloudsmithToken }}"
                afterResponse: "checkTokenResponse"

For successful license requests, the processor captures the returned token and the scenario checks that the token is valid. Artillery records response times, throughput, and response statuses for the run.

Artillery

The test is intended to exceed PyGuard's limit of 100 attempts in a 60-second window, to verify that the protection is enforced under load. For more details on running and interpreting the load test, see the README.

docs.title: MCP Gateway
docs.text:
The Docker MCP Gateway provides the connection between the AI development client and the configured MCP servers.

It manages access to the available MCP tools and forwards tool requests to the appropriate server. This allows the AI client to interact with Grafana without implementing the Grafana API integration itself.

The gateway is managed through Docker Desktop's MCP Toolkit. Depending on the client configuration, the client can communicate with the gateway through a supported MCP transport, such as standard input/output (STDIO).

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text:
The Grafana MCP Server exposes Grafana functionality as MCP tools. It translates supported MCP tool calls into requests to the Grafana HTTP API.

Depending on the server implementation and enabled tools, these operations can include:

  • Listing and inspecting dashboards.
  • Reading dashboard configurations.
  • Creating or updating dashboards.
  • Inspecting data sources and executing supported queries.

The server requires an appropriate Grafana URL and authentication credentials. Dashboard modifications also require sufficient Grafana permissions.

Grafana remains part of the existing Docker Compose application. It provides the dashboards and visualizations used to monitor the application.

The Grafana MCP Server communicates with Grafana through its HTTP API. The existing InfluxDB integration remains responsible for supplying the monitoring data used by dashboard panels.

MCP Catalog

Browse the Docker MCP Catalog to discover available MCP servers.

docs.title: MCP Landscape
docs.text:
Docker Inc. offers an extended configuration guide for setting up Docker Desktop an it's MCP Toolkit.

Enable the MCP Toolkit

  1. Start Docker Desktop.
  2. Open Settings and locate the MCP Toolkit option under the available features.
  3. Enable the toolkit and apply the settings.

Add the Grafana MCP Server

  1. Open the MCP Toolkit interface.
  2. Navigate to the catalog tab.
  3. Search for Grafana.
  4. Add the Grafana MCP Server to a dedicated profile for this project.

Configure the Grafana MCP Server

  1. Open the server configuration.
  2. Configure the Grafana URL and service account token.
  3. Grafana URL: http://host.docker.internal:3001
  4. Grafana API Key: *** (can be taken from the instruction of the README )

Grafana Configuration

The Grafana MCP Server runs in a separate Docker container, so localhost would refer to that container—not the host running Grafana. host.docker.internal lets it reach the host, where Grafana is published on port 3001. If the MCP Server joins the Compose network, use http://grafana:3000 instead.

The URL depends on where the MCP Server runs, e.g. when the mcp server joins the compose.

http://grafana:3000

Configure the MCP Gateway

The Docker MCP Gateway provides the connection between the AI client and the configured MCP servers. When using Docker Desktop's MCP Toolkit, the gateway runs in the background.

Create or select the project-specific profile containing the Grafana MCP Server. Note the profile identifier because the VS Code configuration can reference it explicitly.

Launch the gateway

The following command starts the gateway with that profile and is shown for understanding: VS Code will launch the gateway through its MCP configuration, so a separate terminal process is not normally required.

docker mcp gateway run --profile <your-profile>

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Configure the Gateway

Visual Studio Code can connect to MCP servers through its agent configuration. In this setup, VS Code connects to the Docker MCP Gateway rather than configuring the Grafana MCP Server directly. Open the project in VS Code. Create or update .vscode/mcp.json in the project root.

{
  "servers": {
    "MCP_DOCKER": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "docker",
      "args": [ "mcp", "gateway", "run", "--profile", "<your-profile>" ]
    }
  }
}

The servers object defines the MCP server connection. The command invokes the Docker CLI. The args select the gateway and the configured profile. The stdio transport allows VS Code to communicate with the gateway through standard input and output.

This configuration assumes that the Docker CLI is available in the VS Code environment and that the configured profile exposes the Grafana MCP Server.

Inspect the MCP Tools

Within Docker Desktop you can open the Grafana MCP Server to view its available tools.

In VS Code, open Chat, click Configure Tools in the chat input, then expand MCP_DOCKER to see the tools exposed through the gateway.

Tool Availability

Tool names and availability depend on the installed server version and its configuration. Use the tools actually listed in the current MCP session.

docs.title: Bootstrapping
docs.text:
Bootstrap the Services

This section demonstrates the complete workflow. The services run in Docker Compose, Grafana displays the dashboard, and the AI agent applies changes through MCP.

Open a terminal in the project root and start the application.

# Build images when required and start the Compose services.
docker compose up -d --build

# Check service status.
docker compose ps

Wait until Grafana and the required application services are ready. The existing Compose configuration defines a health check for InfluxDB and makes Grafana depend on that health check.

The MCP Server is managed separately by Docker Desktop unless you have explicitly added it to the Compose project.

Open Grafana

Open the Grafana interface in a browser:

http://localhost:3001

Sign in using the credentials configured for the Grafana instance. Open the dashboard you want to modify.

Keep this browser tab open while working in VS Code. It provides a direct way to verify the changes after the agent applies them.

Ask the Agent to Modify the Dashboard

Open the AI chat in VS Code and confirm that the Grafana MCP tools are available. Select an existing dashboard and provide a specific instruction.

For example:

Inspect the existing Grafana dashboard using the available Grafana
MCP tools.

Add a time-series panel showing backend request failures over time.
Use the existing data source and follow the query conventions already
used by the dashboard.

Keep the change minimal. Do not create a new dashboard or modify
unrelated panels.

Inspect the current dashboard first. Apply the smallest supported
change, save it, and report which panel was added and which query
was used.

Review the proposed operation before allowing changes to a shared or production dashboard.

Verify the Changes in Real Time

Return to the Grafana browser tab and refresh the dashboard if the updated panel is not displayed automatically.

Verify that:

  1. The new panel appears in the intended dashboard.
  2. The panel uses the expected data source.
  3. The query returns meaningful results for the selected time range.
  4. The panel title, visualization type, and layout are correct.
  5. Existing panels remain unchanged.

If the panel is empty, inspect the query, available measurements, time range, and data source configuration. An empty panel does not necessarily mean that the MCP connection failed.

Repeat the process with another targeted change once the first modification is verified.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This bonus chapter follows one small package through the evolution of Python project configuration. It starts with Python 1.6 and distutils, then moves through metadata-only dependency hints, early setuptools, pinned requirements files, setup.cfg, and finally a modern pyproject.toml workflow. The goal is to show how each configuration style worked, why the ecosystem changed, and which ideas still shape current Python packaging practices.
